scenario.brief: You have a task that needs doing this week: preparing a client-facing summary report. You could do it yourself (30 min, guaranteed quality) or delegate it to a capable but newer team member (they'd need 90 min and some guidance, but it's a good growth opportunity for them).
scenario.context: Delegation decisions are rarely about who can do it fastest — they're about what builds team capability over time.

steps.title: Making the Call
steps.prompt: What's the strongest reasoning for this decision?
options: Always do it yourself if you can do it faster and better
Delegate it, since the time cost now is a reasonable investment in the team member's growth, as long as you can review it before it goes to the client
Delegate it and send it to the client without reviewing, to fully hand off ownership
Never delegate anything client-facing, regardless of the team member's capability
steps.reasoning: Delegating with a review step balances the real goal (developing the team member's capability) against the real risk (client-facing quality) — this is what makes delegation sustainable rather than either overly cautious (never delegating) or reckless (no review at all).
steps.tip: When delegating something client-facing for the first time, keep a review step in the process — it protects quality while still giving the team member real ownership of the work itself.
steps.mistake: Always doing it yourself because it's faster in the moment optimizes for this week's efficiency at the cost of ever building a team member's capability — a manager who never delegates limits their own team's growth and their own ability to scale.
steps.recommendation: Frame delegation explicitly as a growth opportunity when assigning it — telling the team member 'this is client-facing, so let's do a review together before it goes out' sets clear, supportive expectations.

steps.title: Assigning the Task
steps.prompt: Write the message (2-3 sentences) you'd send delegating this task.
steps.modelAnswer: I'd like you to take the lead on this week's client summary report — it's client-facing, so let's plan for me to review it with you before it goes out, but I want you to own the drafting and structure. Take a look at last month's version as a reference, and let's touch base Wednesday to review before Friday's deadline. This is a good chance to get more reps on client communication.
steps.reasoning: A strong delegation message clearly assigns real ownership (drafting and structure), sets the review checkpoint expectation upfront (not as a surprise later), gives a helpful reference point, and names why this is a valuable opportunity — this combination builds trust and sets the team member up to succeed.
steps.tip: Set the review checkpoint expectation at the time of assignment, not as a last-minute addition — it feels very different to a team member to know from the start that a review is part of the process, versus being told at the last minute that their work needs checking.
steps.mistake: Delegating without any reference material or context ('just do the report') leaves a newer team member guessing at expectations, increasing both their stress and the chance the review step reveals major issues.
steps.recommendation: Explicitly name the growth value of the task ('good chance to get more reps on client communication') — it reframes the task as an opportunity rather than just an assignment.

outcome.reflectionPrompt: What's a task you currently do yourself that you could delegate as a growth opportunity for someone else? What's stopping you?
